needs: profile conflict default (odrl:conflict odrl:prohibit on the DPROD profile)
notes: Extracted unchanged except the five anonymous rules are named rule:audit-*. odrl:conflict is absent as in DPROD, so the profile default (odrl:prohibit) applies. The retention obligation is the interesting structure: its constraint reads a request-source operand (ex:retentionPeriod), so inside a duty it is a guard read against the request (due2-workflows.md §5.2) — DPROD's activation condition (D-ACTIVATE) — and the obligation is in force for requests whose stated retention period exceeds P7Y. It has no dprod:subjectOfDuty, so its bearer is the request subject (due2-profiles.md §6), and no deadline, so it is never violated. The duration comparison is the other point: P8Y against P7Y is decidable (both year-month); P730D against P7Y is not (mixed kinds, due2-profiles.md §4) — the operand is invalid, the guard U, the obligation's status unknown. DPROD's apply returns false for incomparable operands (§6.2), so the duty condition is false there — the same disagreement as exception 1, here on a guard: due2 keeps the question open, DPROD answers it. DPROD duty collection (§7.2 step 1): odrl:delete never matches a read, so the retention duty is never collected; ex:export matches only an export request. DPROD Σ assumed: Σ₀ with clock = request.at; dprod_expected uses the intended §7.4 reading (request ⊑ rule).

scenarios.name: compliance read of an eight-year retention

expected.why: rule:audit-read applies (purpose = compliance) and no prohibition matches read (modify and export are both outside). Permit. The retention obligation is in force: the read permission matches the request, and its guard holds — P8Y > P7Y, both year-month durations, decidable. No deletion witness, and with no deadline the duty is never violated: outstanding, with the request subject as bearer.

scenarios.dprod_expected: Permit (delete never matches read, so the duty is neither collected nor activated; the permission is active)

scenarios.name: compliance read of a two-year retention

expected.why: The read is permitted as in scenario 1, but the retention guard is false (P2Y is not > P7Y), so the obligation is not in force and is not reported: no deletion is owed for a retention within the limit. Permit, no obligations.

scenarios.dprod_expected: Permit (the duty's activation condition is false, so it stays Pending; and it is never collected for a read)

scenarios.name: read without stating the purpose

expected.why: The purpose operand is missing, so the permission is U; no prohibition matches read, so nothing else can decide it. Completing purpose = compliance permits and any other value does not: Indeterminate. The retention obligation is in force (the read permission matches, constraints aside; guard P8Y > P7Y holds) and outstanding.

scenarios.dprod_expected: Failure(MissingValue odrl:purpose) (due2 decides more often, due2-profiles.md §8.2)

scenarios.name: retention stated in days against a limit in years

expected.why: The permission is definite (purpose = compliance) and nothing denies the read: Permit. The retention guard is U: P730D is a day-time duration, P7Y a year-month one, and gt is undefined across kinds (due2-profiles.md §4) — the operand is invalid, not false, so the constraint is U and the obligation in force is reported unknown. Whether a 730-day retention exceeds seven years is a real question with a real answer (it does, barely), but it is not decidable from these two terms, and due2 says so rather than guessing.

scenarios.dprod_expected: Permit (the duty is never collected for a read; its condition would evaluate apply(gt, P730D, P7Y) = false — the incomparable-operands reading of due2-profiles.md §8.2 exception 1)

expected.why: rule:audit-no-export matches ex:export by equality; ex:export also sits under odrl:distribute, but that only adds nothing here. The read permission does not match (export is not below read). A surviving, applying prohibition: Deny. The retention obligation is not in force — no permission or prohibition of the policy matches an export, which is what in force turns on (§5.2).
